title: Baylor
description: Replacing a 1950s ranch house in La Jolla Village called for restraint. The neighborhood is famously resistant to new construction, and the design needed to earn its place without confrontation. The solution drew on the early modernism of Irving Gill with clean cubic geometries, an emphasis on courtyard living, and a material palette suited to the Southern California climate. The client first envisioned the house as a vacation retreat and eventually as a permanent home designed for aging in place, with enough room for his three adult children and future grandchildren.

The house is composed of two double story volumes connected by a glass bridge. A two-story trellis between them creates a filtered-light outdoor foyer, inspired by the Case Study House tradition, that serves as the main arrival moment before branching left to the entrance and right to the garage with gym and storage above. Inside, a stair and entry hall lead to the great room, with an open kitchen, living room, and direct access to the pool. At street level, a family room doubles as a future ground-floor primary suite for the owners as they age, alongside a third guest suite and adjacent bath. Two bedroom suites occupy the second floor, connected by the bridge to a primary suite with full bath, separate closets, and an ocean-view deck. A pool with spa and a covered outdoor kitchen anchor the rear yard. The facades alternate wood and cement plaster between floors and between volumes, creating a dynamic material exchange that keeps the cubic forms from reading as static.

title: Atherton Residence II
description: Set back from the street at the end of a tree-lined drive, this 13,500-square-foot residence announces itself gradually: a sweeping approach that curves to reveal a formally composed double-gabled house evoking the substance of a classic American manor. Designed for a tech executive with a large and active family, the house is organized in an L-shape around a generous garden, with the forecourt providing a proper arrival sequence before the three-car garage tucks away at the side.

The ground floor is built for life at scale. A formal living room, dining room, and great room with a chef’s kitchen and walk-through pantry wrap the garden on three sides, with sliding glass doors opening the interior to the landscape at nearly every turn. A grandparents’ suite on this level ensures the extended family is always comfortably part of the household. Below grade, the basement opens through large sliding glass doors to the pool and spa, and houses a full sports bar; wellness center with gym, steam room, sauna, and massage room; home theater; and guest quarters. A separate ADU accommodates additional overflow. On the second floor, three bedroom suites flank a capacious primary suite with his-and-hers closets, a private study, and an outdoor terrace. The program totals five bedrooms, six full baths, two powder rooms, two laundry rooms, a wine cellar and bar, game room, library, and a 786-square-foot detached ADU.

title: Atherton Residence I
description: An immense grove of redwoods defines this Atherton property, and from the earliest design conversations, those trees became the generative idea for the house. Two tower-like volumes frame a formal entry bridge that crosses a dramatic water feature, the sound of water threading nature into the arrival sequence. Wood cladding throughout speaks directly to the color and texture of the surrounding trunks.

The ground floor distributes formal and informal life with ease: a living room and library flank the entry on one side, a formal dining room and expansive great room with open kitchen, family room, and casual dining on the other. A secondary pantry and an au pair suite complete the service wing. Four bedroom suites occupy the second floor, the primary positioned in the most prominent location and outfitted with a generously scaled closet, a large bathroom, and a private study. Nearby, a smaller family sitting room offers a place for quieter, more intimate gathering. The basement holds a full entertainment level: media room, billiards, guest suite, massage room, gym, and a sports bar. Outside, a one-bedroom ADU doubles as a pool house, paired with a full outdoor kitchen and a large covered loggia scaled for dinner parties.

title: Churchill Residence
description: This unusual design is based around the strict feng shui precepts of a master based in Taiwan: orienting the house along the north south access, centering the layout, determining dates of construction, and carefully arranging and locating the rooms in good energy sectors.

This multi-generational concept is designed for entertaining. Located on a sloped lot, the entry level features a living/dining room with kitchen, a primary suite that opens to an outdoor terrace with infinity edge pool, and a media room with direct access to the hillside courtyard. The second level contains a family room with kitchenette, study, an en suite, two additional bedrooms, a gym, and a three-car garage.
The client wanted a house that was modern and warm, resulting in the use of muted colors and natural materials, such as wood trellises and screens.

title: Upper Happy Valley ADU
description: We designed this guest suite as a welcoming retreat for the wife’s parents, blending comfort and contemporary craftsmanship into a compact living environment. Defined by its sculptural circular form and Japanese-inspired shou sugi ban cladding, the home seamlessly connects to the main house through the same richly textured finish, as if it had always been there. The distinctive shape softens the architectural presence while maximizing natural light and spatial flow within an efficient footprint. Thoughtfully integrated above the garage, without sacrificing valuable yard space, the design supports multigenerational living while maintaining privacy and independence for both households.

title: Aspegren
description: This Eichler home required careful handling as expansive soil had produced a significant foundation crack, years of deferred maintenance had taken their toll, and the clients wanted both a major remodel and a new ADU, all without losing the character that makes an Eichler an Eichler.

Privacy from neighboring properties was the primary organizing concern, and the solution was to turn the backyard into a courtyard. The ADU was positioned to form the courtyard’s back wall, creating an enclosed outdoor room that the main house now wraps and faces. The ADU itself follows a dumbbell plan with a great room at one end, a bedroom suite at the other, connected by a glass library bridge that fills the structure with light while keeping the two halves distinct.

title: Stoner Pool
description: This pavilion completes a comprehensive remodel of a Sonoma wine estate, resolving a longstanding problem: the existing pool was too remote from the main house to support easy entertaining. The design had to work around a mature stand of oak trees and sit lightly within an established garden landscape.

Taking its cues from the main residence, which had been reimagined in an English Cottage idiom, the pool house is organized as a split structure. At the center, a covered outdoor loggia with kitchen and fireplace serves as an open-air living room, with a custom louver system providing shade on demand. The loggia is bookended on one side by a guest bedroom suite with full bath, and on the other by a hangout room with sliding doors opening to a deck with long views down the valley, ideal for a cocktail hour or a movie night. Steep overhanging rooflines and shingle cladding echo the main house, while steel windows and refined interior finishes keep the language distinctly modern.

title: Portola Valley Residence
description: The clients wanted to remodel their poorly laid out mid-century home. Having been added onto several times, it no longer worked for their active lifestyle. A majority of their time was spent in their 10-foot wide, hilly backyard. After much thought on how to upgrade the existing structure, it became obvious that tearing down and relocating the house 25-feet to the east, at the edge of the hillside, would maximize the rear yard and give the client the indoor/outdoor lifestyle they desired.

The new house is a simple, rectilinear plan, laid out in a continuous sequence. On the ground floor is the entry, formal living and dining rooms, TV room/den, guest quarters, and artist studio. The primary suite, two children’s bedroom, and man cave make up the second floor, with a covered outdoor-sitting room and kitchen, off the den, providing another year-round living space. To create a treehouse effect, large sliding doors and panoramic windows frame backyard views and the downslope grove of trees.

title: La Senda Residence
description: Radical remodel of a 1960’s rancher.

This existing Hillsborough house had an amazing hillside view, reached by a long downslope driveway. However, the house was in terrible shape and had a difficult, reverse plan layout with no visible front door. Keeping the existing footprint, we completely re-conceptualized and transformed it into a five bedroom, five bathroom house.

Now, a new parking court with front door clearly distinguishes the entry, which is further emphasized by the new staircase. Seamlessly integrated into the foyer, the stairs capture views of the valley, encouraging guests to explore the house. The first level is comprised of sleeping quarters and a study. The second level is dedicated to entertaining with formal living and dining spaces, a great room with open kitchen, and guest quarters. Large balconies extend rooms, providing ample outdoor space. Below the first floor, a former crawl space will be fully excavated to gain a rec room that will open directly onto a pool area, and second guest quarters.
The design transforms a mundane rancher into an architectural gem and was fully supported by the ARB of Hillsborough.

title: Cass Lee Residence
description: Under construction. Completing in 2025.
Rising from a six-acre burnt parcel in Ukiah, this multi-building compound replaces a 1940’s ranch-style house that succumbed to the 2018 Mendocino Complex fire.

We designed this residence as a year-round retreat for family and friends. We oriented the great room, with large open kitchen, to maximize the views of the vineyard and ridge beyond. Sliding doors open to a covered patio which offers unobstructed access to the outdoors. On each side of the great room are identical en suites, angled to optimize the view, with the leftover voids entry points for the reading room and breakfast nook.

We stacked a third bedroom suite on top of the north suite, creating a siloed-tower counterpoint to this otherwise barn-like building. Opposite the covered patio, a pool and adjacent pool house offer respite in the hot summers.
To round out the compound, an ADU and separate drying barn, will be completed in 2025.

title: Bonny Doon Retreat
description: Set on 125-acres of forested land, defined by redwoods and distant views of the Pacific, we were invited to design a private family compound as part of a competition.

Paramount to our design was creating an intimate sense of place while maintaining the rustic, unspoiled setting. The parcel called for something organic; however, the family wanted a modern home that maintained a glamping-feel that would inspire play and adventure.

Starting with the idea of a wellness retreat, individual cabanas evolved into a series of interconnected pavilions arranged around a central meadow. Each pavilion was inspired by its specific location. The first — a three-story tree house — contains the main entry, guest and primary suites, and a “bird’s nest” study above. The second, a sky pavilion, features the great room with kitchen and dining areas oriented towards the ocean. The third, the moss pavilion, is nestled in the leaf-covered oak forest, and houses the children’s bedrooms. The fourth, a water pavilion pool house, encompasses the guest quarters and spa.
The limited palette of Corten steel, board-formed concrete, and glass blends into the forested site. Prone to wildfires, materials were chosen for their fire-resistance attributes.

title: BCLT Mesa
description: Worker housing and agricultural co-op

For years, dozens of agricultural workers and their families had been living on Tacherra Ranch in substandard conditions – basically, these essential workers were living in sheds and storage containers without running water or sewer. The site had been red-tagged by the County of Marin for numerous code violations; however, due to the overwhelming need for worker housing, the site was not condemned.

To alleviate these dire conditions, the BCLT, local Bolinas community, and the County provided emergency funding for a temporary RV park for these roughly 60 people, along with a plan to create permanent housing.

Ultimately, the County wants to establish an agricultural coop and build six modular family homes for these workers, as allowed by the Williamson Act. The plans calls for four individual 2-bedroom suites with a common kitchen, and two 2-bedroom units. The plan also entails a shared dry storage barn, community kitchen, and gathering room, as well as a tractor repair and workshop building. Moreover, the project is proposing a daycare facility that would service the entire community.
Currently, the project is aggregating funding.

title: Habitat for Humanity
description: Affordable housing project in partnership with the Bolinas Community Land Trust (BCLT).

Addressing the desperate need for workforce housing, the Bolinas Community Land Trust (BCLT) embarked on an ambitious plan to build eight units of housing in Downtown Bolinas — six 3-bed / 1-bath units and two 2-bed / 1-bath units, each with outdoor terraces. Wedged between a historic saloon and a single-family home, we placed four units in a three-story front building, with offices for the BCLT at street level, and a separate, three-story back building with four units above parking to reduce the scale.

Designed to blend with the funky character of this notable alternative community, the building is clad in white clapboard and weathered cedar, with the side exterior wall earmarked for an artist mural.
Habitat for Humanity took over the affordable housing project and will be offering these units for sale.
The groundbreaking took place October 15, 2025.

title: UC Berkeley Eyewear Retail Center
description: Part of the new UC Berkeley Herbert Wertheim School of Optometry and Vision Science.

Having experience mostly in institutional work versus market retail, TEF, the Architect of Record contracted us to design the retail portion of the project. The goal was to provide an in-store experience that would remain stylish and up-to- date, while providing ample room as a teaching facility in order to offer hands-on retail experience for the students. Designed as a family care practice, the displays and waiting area are playful yet durable, while continuing to be healthcare focused. A nod to the university’s mascot, the waiting lounge is designed as a den-like cave area, working within the Cal Bears theme.
